advent: The arrival or start of something important.
aesthetic: Connected with beauty and how things look.
affable: Friendly and easy to talk to.
aggravate: To make a bad situation worse; informally, to annoy someone.
agile: Able to move or think quickly and easily.
alienate: To make someone feel unwelcome or turn them against you.
allegation: A claim that someone did something wrong, not yet proved.
alleviate: To make pain or a problem less severe.
aloof: Cool and distant; not friendly or involved.
altruistic: Caring about others and helping them without wanting anything back.
ambivalent: Having mixed feelings: part of you wants something and part of you doesn't.
amenable: Willing to accept or be persuaded.
anecdote: A short, interesting story about something that really happened.
animosity: Strong dislike or hostility between people.
anomaly: Something different from what is normal or expected.
antagonise: To make someone angry or hostile towards you.
apathy: Not caring or not being interested at all.
appease: To calm someone down by giving them what they want.
apprehensive: Worried that something bad might happen.
arduous: Very hard and tiring, needing a lot of effort.
articulate: Able to express ideas clearly and well.
aspire: To have a strong wish to achieve something (aspire to).
assertive: Confident in saying what you want or think, without being rude.
astute: Clever at understanding situations and people, and using that to your advantage.
audacious: Boldly daring, taking risks others wouldn't.
austerity: Strict cuts in spending, especially by a government; also a plain, simple way of life.
authentic: Real and genuine, not a copy or pretend.
autonomy: The freedom to make your own decisions or govern yourself.
banal: Boring and ordinary, with nothing new.
belligerent: Aggressive and ready to argue or fight.
benevolent: Kind and wanting to help others.
benign: Gentle and harmless; of a medical lump, not cancerous.
bewildered: Very confused and unsure what to do.
blatant: Very obvious and done without trying to hide it, usually something bad.
brazen: Shamelessly open about doing something wrong.
brevity: Using few words; also being short in time.
bureaucracy: A system with many officials and rules, often slow and complicated.
cajole: To gently persuade someone with flattery or promises.
callous: Cruel and not caring about other people's feelings.
candid: Honest and direct, even about difficult things.
capricious: Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and without reason.
catalyst: Something that makes a change happen faster.
caveat: A warning that something may not be quite as it seems.
chronic: Lasting a long time or keeps coming back, usually a problem or illness.
circumvent: To find a clever way round a rule or problem.
clandestine: Done secretly, often because it's not allowed.
cliché: A phrase or idea used so often it has lost its effect.
cognitive: Connected with thinking, learning and remembering.
collateral: Something valuable promised to a lender in case you can't repay a loan.
compelling: So interesting or convincing that you pay attention or agree.
complacent: Too pleased with yourself to notice dangers or try harder.
concede: To admit, often unwillingly, that something is true; also to accept defeat.
concise: Short and clear, with no unnecessary words.
condescending: Treating people as if they are less clever or important than you.
condone: To accept or allow behaviour that is wrong.
conducive: Making it easier for something to happen (conducive to).
confide: To tell someone a secret or private feeling because you trust them.
conjecture: A guess based on incomplete information.
conscientious: Careful and hard-working, wanting to do things properly.
contingency: Something that might happen, which you plan for just in case.
convoluted: Very complicated and hard to follow.
cordial: Friendly but polite and a little formal.
corroborate: To support a claim with new evidence.
credible: Believable and able to be trusted.
culminate: To reach a final, often dramatic, point (culminate in).
cumbersome: Large, heavy or slow and difficult to use.
cynical: Believing that people only act for selfish reasons.
daunting: Making you feel nervous because it seems difficult.
debilitating: Making someone very weak or unable to function.
decadent: Enjoying too much luxury and pleasure, in a way some see as morally weak.
deference: Polite respect, especially accepting someone else's opinion.
defer: To delay something until later; also to accept someone else's judgement (defer to).
deflect: To turn attention, blame or a question away from yourself.
delegate: To give part of your work or power to someone else.
deliberate: Done on purpose; also slow and careful.
delusion: A false belief that someone holds firmly.
demeanour: The way someone looks and behaves.
demise: The end or failure of something; formally, someone's death.
deplete: To use up a large part of something.
deprive: To take away something someone needs (deprive of).
deride: To make fun of someone or something as worthless.
deter: To make someone decide not to do something, often through fear.
devastate: To destroy something completely; also to make someone extremely upset.
dexterity: Skill with your hands, or quick clever thinking.
dichotomy: A sharp division between two opposite things.
discern: To notice or understand something that isn't obvious.
disclose: To make information known that was private or secret.
discrepancy: A difference between things that should match.
disdain: The feeling that someone or something isn't worth your respect.
disparity: A big, often unfair, difference between things.
dispel: To make a feeling or belief go away.
disrupt: To interrupt and stop something from working normally.
dissent: Disagreement with an official or popular opinion.
dogmatic: Sure your beliefs are right and unwilling to consider others.
dubious: Doubtful, or probably not honest or true.
eclectic: Made up of a wide variety of styles or sources.
elicit: To draw out a reaction or information from someone.
eloquent: Speaking or writing in a clear, moving and persuasive way.
elusive: Hard to find, catch, understand or achieve.
embark: To start something new and important (embark on); also to get on a ship.
embellish: To add details to make something more attractive or interesting, sometimes untrue ones.
empathy: The ability to understand and share someone else's feelings.
endeavour: A serious attempt to do something.
endorse: To publicly say you support someone or something.
enigma: Someone or something mysterious and hard to understand.
entrepreneur: Someone who starts a business, taking financial risks.
ephemeral: Lasting only a very short time.
equitable: Fair and reasonable, treating everyone equally.
eradicate: To get rid of something completely.
esoteric: Understood only by a small group with special knowledge.
euphemism: A gentler word used instead of one that might upset people.
exacerbate: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
exasperate: To annoy someone a lot, especially when they can't do anything about it.
exemplary: So good it's an example for others.
exonerate: To show officially that someone is not to blame.
expedite: To make a process happen faster.
extravagant: Spending or using much more than is sensible.
facade: The front of a building; also a false appearance that hides the truth.
fallacy: A false belief, or a mistake in reasoning.
fickle: Changing your mind or loyalties often.
flagrant: Shockingly obvious, usually about breaking a rule.
flamboyant: Confident, colourful and showy, wanting to be noticed.
foster: To help something develop; also to look after a child who isn't yours for a time.
frugal: Careful to spend very little money.
futile: Having no chance of success; pointless.
galvanise: To shock or excite people into taking action.
gauge: To judge or measure something, such as a feeling or amount.
gregarious: Enjoying being with other people; sociable.
grievance: A feeling or complaint that you've been treated unfairly.
gullible: Too ready to believe what people tell you, so easily tricked.
hamper: To make it harder for something to happen or move.
haphazard: Done without a plan or order.
hinder: To slow down or make something difficult.
hindsight: Understanding a situation only after it has happened.
holistic: Looking at the whole of something rather than separate parts.
hostile: Unfriendly and ready to argue or fight.
hubris: Too much pride and self-confidence, often leading to failure.
hypocrisy: Saying one thing but doing the opposite, or pretending to have beliefs you don't.
impartial: Fair, not supporting one side more than another.
impeccable: Perfect, with no faults at all.
impede: To slow down or block progress.
imperative: Extremely important and urgent; something that must be done.
impetus: Something that pushes a process forward or makes it happen faster.
incessant: Never stopping, usually in an annoying way.
incisive: Clear, sharp and quick to get to the important point.
incongruous: Strange because it doesn't fit with what's around it.
indifferent: Not caring or interested either way.
indignant: Angry because you feel you've been treated unfairly.
indulge: To let yourself enjoy something special; also to let someone have what they want.
inept: Lacking skill; clumsy at doing something.
inertia: A lack of energy or will to change or act.
innate: Present from birth; natural rather than learned.
insatiable: Always wanting more; impossible to satisfy.
insinuate: To suggest something bad in an indirect, unpleasant way.
insipid: Having little taste, interest or energy; dull.
instigate: To make something start, often trouble or an official process.
intimidate: To frighten someone so they do what you want.
intricate: Having many small parts or details that fit together.
intuitive: Based on feeling rather than reasoning; also easy to use without instructions.
inundate: To give someone so much of something that they can't deal with it all.
irony: When what happens is the opposite of what you'd expect; also saying the opposite of what you mean, for effect.
jeopardise: To put something at risk of being harmed or lost.
juxtapose: To place things side by side so their differences stand out.
lament: To express sadness or regret about something.
latent: Present but hidden, not yet developed or shown.
lenient: Less strict in punishing than expected.
leverage: Power or influence you can use to get what you want; in finance, borrowing to invest more.
lucid: Clear and easy to understand; also thinking clearly.
magnanimous: Generous and kind, especially towards a rival or someone who lost.
malicious: Meaning to hurt or upset someone.
mandatory: Required by a rule or law; compulsory.
meticulous: Extremely careful about every small detail.
mitigate: To make something bad less severe.
myriad: A very large number of things.
naive: Too trusting because of a lack of experience.
negligent: Not taking proper care when you should.
nonchalant: Calm and relaxed, seeming not to care.
nostalgia: A warm, slightly sad longing for the past.
nuance: A small, subtle difference in meaning, feeling or colour.
oblivious: Not noticing what's happening around you.
obscure: Not well known; also hard to understand.
obsolete: No longer used because something newer exists.
obstinate: Stubbornly refusing to change your mind.
ominous: Suggesting that something bad is going to happen.
opaque: Not see-through; also hard to understand.
opportunistic: Taking advantage of chances as they come, often selfishly.
optimal: The best or most effective possible.
ostensibly: Seemingly or officially, though the real reason may be different.
ostentatious: Showing off wealth or importance to impress people.
paradox: Something that seems impossible because it contains two opposite facts, yet may be true.
pedantic: Too concerned with small details or rules.
pensive: Thinking deeply, often a little sadly.
perceptive: Quick to notice and understand things.
peripheral: At the edge; not central or very important.
pernicious: Harmful, especially in a gradual, hidden way.
perpetual: Never ending or changing; happening again and again.
pertinent: Directly connected with the subject; relevant.
pervasive: Spread through every part of something.
placate: To calm someone and make them less angry.
plausible: Seeming likely to be true or reasonable.
poignant: Making you feel sad in a deep, touching way.
pragmatic: Dealing with things sensibly and practically, based on what works.
precarious: Not safe or stable; likely to fall or fail.
precedent: An earlier event or decision used as an example for later ones.
predicament: A difficult situation that's hard to get out of.
premise: An idea that an argument or plan is based on.
prerogative: A right or privilege that belongs to a particular person or group.
presumptuous: Doing something you have no right to do, too confidently.
pretentious: Trying to seem more important, clever or cultured than you are.
prevalent: Common or widespread at a particular time or place.
proactive: Acting early to make things happen or prevent problems, rather than waiting.
procrastinate: To keep putting off something you should do.
prolific: Producing a lot of work or results.
prominent: Important and well known; also easy to see.
propensity: A natural tendency to behave in a certain way.
prudent: Sensible and careful, thinking about the future.
quandary: A state of not knowing what to decide.
rapport: A friendly understanding between people that makes communication easy.
rationale: The reasons behind a decision or belief.
reciprocate: To do or feel the same in return.
rectify: To correct something that is wrong.
redundant: No longer needed; in the UK, also losing your job because it's no longer needed.
reiterate: To say something again for emphasis.
relentless: Never stopping or getting less intense.
remorse: A strong feeling of regret for doing something wrong.
renounce: To formally give up a belief, right or claim.
repercussion: An effect, usually bad, that comes later from an action.
resilient: Able to recover quickly after difficulties.
reticent: Not willing to share your thoughts or feelings.
retrospect: In retrospect: thinking back on something after it has happened.
revere: To respect and admire someone deeply.
rhetoric: Persuasive speech, often impressive but not very sincere.
robust: Strong and unlikely to break or fail.
rudimentary: Very basic, at the simplest level.
sabotage: To secretly damage something to stop it working or succeeding.
sanction: An official punishment, often against a country; also official permission.
scepticism: Doubt about whether something is true or will work.
serendipity: Finding something good by happy accident, without looking for it.
skew: To make information or results unfair or inaccurate.
sombre: Serious and sad; also dark in colour.
sporadic: Happening now and then, not regularly.
spurious: False, though it may seem true.
stoic: Accepting pain or trouble calmly without complaining.
subtle: Small and not obvious, so you need to look carefully to notice it.
succinct: Saying something clearly in very few words.
superficial: Only on the surface; not deep or thorough.
susceptible: Easily affected or harmed by something.
tangible: Real and clear enough to touch or measure.
tantamount: Almost the same as something worse (tantamount to).
tenacious: Holding on firmly and not giving up.
tentative: Not certain or final; done carefully, unsure.
trajectory: The path something follows as it moves; also the direction a career or trend is going.
transient: Lasting only a short time; passing.
trepidation: Fear or worry about something that is going to happen.
tumultuous: Full of noise, confusion or change.
undermine: To gradually weaken something or someone.
vehement: Showing very strong feeling, especially disagreement.
venerable: Respected because of age, wisdom or long history.
vicarious: Felt through someone else's experience rather than your own.
vigilant: Watching carefully for danger or problems.
vindicate: To prove that someone was right or not to blame.
volatile: Likely to change suddenly and unpredictably.
wary: Careful because you think something might be dangerous or a problem.
whimsical: Playful and unusual, often in a charming way.
zealous: Very enthusiastic and committed, sometimes too much.
